nameStory: This moss gets its "goose neck" name from its distinctive curved stem tips that arch and bend like a goose's neck when the plant is growing actively. The "rough" part comes from the coarse, irregular texture you feel when you run your fingers over a patch of this moss.
description: Rough goose neck moss is a robust, feathery moss that forms loose, sprawling mats across the forest floor. It grows 3-6 inches tall with distinctive arching, curved branch tips that create an elegant feathery appearance. The main stems are thick and sturdy compared to many other mosses, giving the whole plant a somewhat coarse, three-dimensional look rather than lying flat against surfaces.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, feathery mats with distinctively curved, arching branch tips that look like tiny goose necks - this curved appearance is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels noticeably rough and coarse when you run your hand over it, unlike the soft, velvety texture of many other feather mosses

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Individual leaves are triangular and overlapping like shingles, creating a three-ranked pattern that gives stems a distinctly three-sided appearance when viewed closely

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Deep green when moist, turning yellowish-green to bronze when dry, with the color change being quite dramatic between wet and dry conditions

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found on decaying logs, stumps, and organic soil in mature forests - rarely grows directly on rocks or tree bark like many other mosses

habitat: Rough goose neck moss thrives in mature, moist coniferous and mixed forests throughout New England's mountains and hills. Look for it covering rotting logs, old stumps, and rich organic soil in areas that stay consistently humid. It's particularly common in spruce-fir forests at higher elevations and in cool, shaded ravines where the air stays moist year-round.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green growth begins as snow melts, with the characteristic curved branch tips becoming most pronounced. This is when the moss looks most vibrant and the goose-neck curves are easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Maintains steady growth through humid summer months, though may appear somewhat yellower during dry spells. The rough texture is most noticeable when comparing with other mosses.
seasonality.fall: Often develops richer, deeper green colors in the increased moisture of autumn. Sporophytes (capsules) may appear on thin stalks, though this species doesn't reproduce by spores as frequently as others.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover, appearing bronze-green to yellowish. The sturdy stems and distinctive growth pattern make it identifiable even in dormant conditions.

funFact: This moss can actually change its growth direction mid-stream - if a branch tip gets buried under falling leaves or debris, it will curve upward and around obstacles like a plant periscope, always seeking the perfect light and moisture conditions.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other feather mosses like stair-step moss, but rough goose neck moss feels noticeably coarser and rougher to the touch, plus those distinctive curved branch tips are unique - remember "rough goose necks" for both the texture and the curved shape.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's related to other "goose neck" plants, this moss gets its name purely from appearance - the curved stems really do look like tiny goose necks when you see them up close, making this one of the more accurately descriptive moss names.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other large feather mosses in the broader family. Unlike the common stair-step moss which has a more regular, ladder-like branching pattern, rough goose neck moss has those distinctive curved tips and much coarser texture. It's also larger and more robust than most other feathery forest floor mosses.
